Physical Therapy Instructions Following Total Knee Replacement

Physical therapy is a cornerstone of recovery after total knee replacement. The exercises and techniques described below are general guidelines. Your physical therapist will provide a personalized program tailored to your specific condition and progress.

Phase 1: Early Recovery (Days 1–14)
Goals: Reduce swelling, restore basic range of motion, establish safe ambulation with assistive device.

Ankle Pumps: While lying down, flex and point your foot up and down repeatedly. Perform 10 repetitions every hour you are awake. This exercise promotes blood circulation and reduces the risk of blood clots.

Quadriceps Sets: Tighten the muscles on the front of your thigh by pressing the back of your knee down into the bed. Hold for 5 seconds. Perform 10 repetitions, 3 times per day.

Straight Leg Raises: While lying on your back with the non-operative leg bent, tighten your thigh muscle on the operative leg and raise it to the height of the opposite knee. Hold for 3 seconds and lower slowly. Perform 10 repetitions, 3 times per day.

Heel Slides: Lying on your back, slide your heel toward your buttocks, bending the knee as far as comfortable. Hold for 5 seconds and straighten. Perform 10 repetitions, 3 times per day. Record how far you can bend your knee each day.

Sitting Knee Flexion: Sit on the edge of a chair and gently bend and straighten your knee using gravity. Attempt to achieve at least 90 degrees of flexion by day 10.

Ambulation with Walker: Walk with your walker on flat surfaces 3 to 4 times per day. Start with short distances (10–20 feet) and gradually increase. Always lead with the operative leg when advancing the walker.

Phase 2: Intermediate Recovery (Weeks 2–6)
Goals: Achieve at least 120 degrees of knee flexion, transition to cane or independent walking, improve strength.

Stationary Cycling: Begin stationary cycling when you have achieved at least 100 degrees of knee flexion. Start with low resistance and a high seat position. Cycle for 5–10 minutes initially, building to 20–30 minutes by week 6.

Mini Squats: Stand holding a stable surface. Perform shallow knee bends (no more than 30–45 degrees of knee flexion). Perform 2 sets of 10, progressing to 3 sets as strength improves.

Step-Ups: Step up onto a 4-inch step with the operative leg leading, then step back down with the non-operative leg leading. Progress to a 6-inch and then 8-inch step as tolerated.

Seated Leg Press: Using gym equipment under therapist supervision, perform gentle seated leg press exercises to strengthen quadriceps and hamstrings.

Phase 3: Advanced Recovery (Weeks 6–12)
Goals: Full functional range of motion, independent walking without assistive device, return to daily activities.

Water Walking: Walking in a pool reduces joint stress while providing resistance training. Begin water walking when cleared by your surgeon (typically after incision is fully healed).

Balance and Proprioception Training: Single-leg balance exercises and balance board activities improve stability and reduce fall risk. Perform under therapist supervision initially.

Gait Training: Work with your therapist to normalize your gait pattern, eliminate limping, and practice navigating stairs, uneven surfaces, and slopes.

General Guidelines:
Do not push through sharp or severe pain. Mild soreness after exercise is normal; sharp pain during exercise is not. Apply ice for 15–20 minutes after exercise sessions to reduce swelling. Inform your physical therapist of any new symptoms or changes in your condition. Maintain your home exercise program consistently for best results.
